items.title: Neuroprotective actions of GLP-1 receptor agonists in Neurodegeneration: From mechanisms to clinical translation.
items.authors: Yalin Lin; Junqi He; Junwen Gong; Jiaxin Chen; Zhiqiang Ke; Fei Cai
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have been explored as potential therapeutics for neurodegenerative disorders, yet a comprehensive integration of their neuroprotective mechanisms across Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and related conditions remains to be consolidated. This review examines the multimodal effects of GLP-1RAs on neuroinflammation, autophagy, mitochondrial function, and protein aggregation, with a focus on translational relevance and alignment between preclinical findings and clinical evidence. METHODOLOGY: A systematic synthesis of preclinical and clinical studies investigating GLP-1RA administration in neurodegenerative disease models and populations was conducted. Studies reporting neuroprotective outcomes and mechanistic pathways were included, and clinical trial data and real-world evidence for AD, PD, Huntington's disease, stroke, diabetic encephalopathy, and peripheral neuropathy were systematically evaluated. RESULTS: Preclinical evidence revealed that GLP-1RAs modulate key pathogenic processes, including amyloid-β and tau pathology, α-synuclein accumulation, neuroinflammatory cascades, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dynamics, endoplasmic reticulum stress, autophagy, and synaptic plasticity. Clinical data provided variable support, with emerging real-world evidence suggesting potential benefits. Novel strategies-such as dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists, enhanced blood-brain barrier penetration, and sustained-release formulations-were identified as promising approaches to improve efficacy, although significant gaps remain between preclinical promise and clinical outcomes. CONCLUSION: This review consolidates evidence that GLP-1RAs exert broad neuroprotective effects through multiple mechanisms, but clinical translation is still evolving. The potential of GLP-1-based therapies as disease-modifying interventions for neurodegeneration warrants further investigation, with particular attention to bridging preclinical and clinical findings and optimizing drug delivery strategies.

items.title: Hypersensitivity to adrenomedullin in post-traumatic headache: a randomized crossover study.
items.authors: Haidar M Al-Khazali; Zahra Hakimzadeh; Anna G Melchior; Berkay Alpay; Ksenija Cucanić; Annette M Fuchs; Messoud Ashina; Håkan Ashina
items.abstract: Adrenomedullin (ADM), a vasoactive member of the calcitonin peptide family with receptor-signalling overlap with calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), has emerged as a candidate therapeutic target in migraine. Given the striking clinical parallels between migraine and persistent post-traumatic headache (PTH), we investigated whether ADM-responsive signalling contributes to migraine-like headache in adults with persistent PTH attributed to mild traumatic brain injury. We conducted a single-centre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-way crossover study in adults with persistent PTH and no pre-trauma history of migraine. On two experimental days separated by at least 7 days, participants received 20-minute intravenous infusions of ADM (19.9 pmol kg⁻¹ min⁻¹) and isotonic saline as the matched inactive comparator (placebo) in randomised sequence. Headache outcomes were recorded for 12 hours. The primary outcome was the within-participant incidence of experimentally induced migraine-like headache. The secondary outcome was the within-participant difference in baseline-corrected area under the curve (AUC) for headache intensity from 0 to 12 hours. Of 158 individuals assessed for eligibility, 21 were randomised, completed both periods and were analysed. Participants had a mean age of 34.3 years, 19 (90%) were female, and 18 (86%) reported a migraine-like phenotype. Migraine-like headache occurred in 17 of 21 participants (81%) after ADM and four of 21 (19%) following placebo. Fourteen participants developed migraine-like only after ADM and one only following placebo, yielding a paired absolute risk difference of 61.9 percentage points (95% CI 29.7-80.6; one-sided P < 0.001; two-sided P = 0.001). Baseline-corrected headache-intensity AUC was higher after ADM than placebo (median 1,110 [IQR 315-2205] versus 420 [-160 to 565]; P = 0.006). Median time to onset of migraine-like headache was 30 minutes after ADM and 390 minutes following placebo. Fifteen participants reported that the ADM-induced headache resembled their usual migraine-like headache episodes, and rescue medication was used by 10 participants after ADM and two after placebo. These findings identify pronounced responsiveness to ADM-linked signalling in persistent PTH and support the ADM pathway as a candidate target for mechanism-based therapeutic development, pending confirmation in independent cohorts and complementary preclinical studies.

items.title: Longitudinal dynamics of the oral microbiota during allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation: an exploratory study with complementary gut microbiota analysis.
items.authors: Yumiko Ohbayashi; Osamu Imataki; Akihiro Takeuchi; Miona Sakaji; Tomoya Ishida; Shumpei Uchida; Makiko Uemura; Haruyuki Nakayama-Imaohji
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The oral microbiota undergoes substantial ecological disruption during allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT), potentially contributing to systemic infections. Although allo-HSCT-associated gut microbiota dysbiosis has been extensively investigated, longitudinal changes in oral microbiota and their relationship with bloodstream infections (BSIs) remain incompletely understood. We therefore aimed to characterize longitudinal changes in oral and gut microbiota and examine their association with BSIs. METHODS: We prospectively analyzed the oral and gut microbiota of 16 adult allo-HSCT recipients using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Salivary and fecal samples were collected before transplantation, on the day of transplantation, during neutropenia, at engraftment, and after engraftment. RESULTS: Six patients developed 11 BSI episodes, with the first episode in each patient occurring at a median of 8 days after transplantation. Staphylococcus haemolyticus was the most common pathogen (7/11 episodes), followed by Enterococcus faecium (2/11 episodes). The oral microbiota underwent marked longitudinal alterations throughout the transplantation period, accompanied by similar changes in the gut microbiota. Differences in microbiota trajectories were observed between patients with and without BSIs despite comparable cumulative antibiotic exposure. Oral-associated genera, including Streptococcus, Fusobacterium, Veillonella, Actinomyces, and Lautropia, were detected in fecal samples, suggesting possible oral-to-gut translocation. CONCLUSIONS: The oral and gut microbiota underwent substantial longitudinal alterations during allo-HSCT. Differences in microbiota dynamics between patients with and without BSIs were not explained solely by antibiotic exposure. These exploratory findings provide insights into the timing of oral and gut microbiota alterations during allo-HSCT and highlight potential relationships between oral and gut microbial changes and BSIs.

items.title: miR-665 Ameliorates Neuroinflammation After Intracerebral Hemorrhage by Modulating Myeloid Cell Polarization via Targeting STAT3.
items.authors: Zhangliang Huang; Yuqi Yang; Bing Sun; Jianing Luo; Yongxiang Yang; Dongbo Zou; Yongquan Cui; Lekai Wang
items.abstract: Background Microglia-mediated neuroinflammation contributes to secondary injury after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), but the role of miR-665 remains unclear.Methods An ICH rat model was established. A combination of techniques, including Neurological scoring, brain water content measurement, histology and molecular assays were employed to assess miR-665, the STAT3/NF-κB pathway, myeloid polarization and inflammation. Stereotaxic miR-665 agomir/antagomir delivery verified its function. The targeting relationship between miR-665 and STAT3 was confirmed by a dual-luciferase reporter assay. In vitro experiments were performed in Hemin-stimulated BV2 cells with miR-665 mimics/inhibitor, followed by flow cytometry detection of cell polarization and inflammatory factor analysis. Rescue experiments with STAT3 overexpression were conducted both in vivo and in vitro.Results After ICH, miR-665 was downregulated andinduced excessive activation of the STAT3/NF-κB signaling axis in peri-hematomal tissue, accompanied by M1-like/pro-inflammatory myeloid cell polarization and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines. Upregulation of miR-665 ameliorated neurological function, reduced brain edema, promoted M2-like/repair-associated polarization, and suppressed inflammation, whereas miR-665 downregulation aggravated injury. Dual-luciferase assay confirmed that miR-665 directly targets STAT3. In vitro, miR-665 overexpression inhibited STAT3 phosphorylation and further suppressed the downstream NF-κB signaling, reversing the Hemin-induced M1-like/pro-inflammatory polarization. STAT3 overexpression counteracted the protective effects of miR-665.Conclusion Downregulated miR-665 after ICH exacerbates neuroinflammation by promoting M1-like/pro-inflammatory myeloid cell polarization via disinhibition of STAT3 and subsequent activation of NF-κB signaling. Upregulating miR-665 exerts neuroprotection by inhibiting STAT3 phosphorylation and facilitating M2-like/repair-associated myeloid cell polarization, highlighting the miR-665/STAT3 regulatory cascade as a promising therapeutic target for post-ICH neuroinflammation.

items.title: Periodontitis as a Modifiable Risk Factor for Dementia: Mechanistic Pathways Linking Oral Inflammation to Neurodegeneration.
items.journal: The Canadian journal of neurological sciences. Le journal canadien des sciences neurologiques
items.authors: Said Nady Makarios; Rohit Shukla; Hariom Yadav; Shalini Jain
items.abstract: Emerging evidence increasingly implicates chronic periodontal disease as a contributor to age-related cognitive decline and dementia, including Alzheimer's disease (AD). Periodontitis is defined by persistent oral microbial dysbiosis, ulcerated gingival epithelium, repeated bacteremia and sustained systemic inflammatory signaling - factors that plausibly influence neuroimmune pathways and cerebrovascular integrity. This review synthesizes findings from epidemiological studies, systematic reviews, mechanistic analyses and experimental models to examine the biological links between oral inflammation and neurodegeneration. Collectively, the literature suggests a stepwise oral-brain axis: first gingival inflammation promotes local and systemic pro-inflammatory cytokine release, second repeated bacteremia allows oral pathogens and microbial byproducts to enter circulation, third these signals and agents access and compromise the blood-brain barrier, then fourth microglia in the brain become primed and hyper-reactive and at last enhanced neuroinflammation accelerates amyloid-β and tau pathology. Although causal inference remains limited by the predominance of observational data, emerging intervention studies and mechanistic evidence suggest that periodontal health is a potentially modifiable factor in dementia prevention strategies.

items.title: Mitochondrial protein import stress augments α-synuclein aggregation and neural damage.
items.authors: Liam P Coyne; Arnav Rana; Xiaowen Wang; Joseph Mauro; Sanaea Bhagwagar; Yumiko Umino; Eduardo C Solessio; Frank Middleton
items.abstract: Genetic and environmental factors are known to converge on mitochondria to cause Parkinson's disease. The underlying mechanism is incompletely understood. In addition to bioenergetic defects, nonbioenergetic pathways have been largely unexplored. Validating the nonbioenergetic mitochondrial stressors as independent pathogenic factors is challenging because most mouse models of mitochondrial stress are confounded by bioenergetic defects. Here, we show that expression of Ant1P.A114P,A123D, previously shown to cause mitochondrial protein import clogging in cultured human cells, does not affect the overall bioenergetic capacity, yet it induces proteostatic stress responses in the cytosol that suggests accumulation of unimported precursor proteins. In a Parkinson's disease model expressing α-synuclein (A53T), Ant1P.A114P,A123D increased the size of α-synuclein aggregates, increased aggregation of mitochondrial preproteins, heightened neuroinflammation, and worsened motor coordination defects. Importantly, we found no evidence of bioenergetic defects in either α-synuclein (A53T) or α-synuclein (A53T) + Ant1P.A114P,A123D mice. These data suggest that Ant1P.A114P,A123D likely induces mitochondrial protein import stress, and contributes to neural damage through cytosolic proteostatic stress and altered aggregation dynamics of neuropathogenic proteins independent of bioenergetics.

items.title: Recent advances on the role of microRNAs in Alzheimer's Disease: Unraveling Mechanisms and Therapeutic Potential.
items.authors: Abolfazl Ardjmand; Seyed Esmaeil Khoshnam; Amirhesam Keshavarz Zarjani; Ali Arjmand; Ghasem Forutan; Sadegh Moradi Vastegani
items.abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are now recognized as key regulators of the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and offer promising opportunities for early detection and treatment. Some miRNAs are responsible for controlling and modulating neuroinflammatory responses, while others directly affect the process of amyloid beta (Aβ) production. Their relative stability in biological fluids supports their potential use in diagnostic panels; however, their diagnostic performance requires further validation before clinical application. From a therapeutic perspective, miRNA antagonists and mimetics have been shown in preclinical studies to reduce amyloid pathology, ameliorate cognitive impairment, and stimulate neurogenesis in animal models of AD. In this review article, we summarize the evidence on the diverse and multifaceted functions of miRNAs in key aspects of AD pathology, including Aβ synthesis via BACE1 and APP regulation, tau aggregation and phosphorylation, APOE4 signaling cascades, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and synaptic plasticity. By linking mechanistic understanding of miRNAs with potential translational applications, miRNA-based strategies may offer promising opportunities for improving the early diagnosis and treatment of AD. However, further preclinical validation and rigorous clinical studies are needed to establish their safety, efficacy, and clinical utility.

items.title: PPARγ at the Nexus of Lipid Metabolism and Neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's Disease: A Longitudinal Multi-omics Analysis.
items.authors: Hao Huixuan; Wang Ruizhe; Hu Chunrong; Wang Na; Dong Tianwai; Yuan Ludan; Luo Wenzhe; Sui Xiaofang
items.abstract: Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) has emerged as an important regulator linking lipid metabolism and neuroimmune responses in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Increasing evidence suggests that disruption of the lipid-immune axis contributes to disease progression and may underlie the heterogeneous therapeutic responses observed with PPARγ-targeted interventions. Experimental studies indicate that PPARγ activation influences multiple biological processes relevant to AD, including lipid homeostasis, mitochondrial function, inflammatory signaling, and amyloid-β clearance. However, the translation of these findings into consistent clinical benefit remains limited by challenges such as poor blood-brain barrier penetration, systemic adverse effects, and disease stage-dependent therapeutic responses. Recent advances in multi-omics technologies and single-cell transcriptomics have provided new insights into the context-dependent roles of PPARγ in different neural cell populations, highlighting dynamic interactions between lipid metabolism, neuroinflammation, and cellular function throughout AD progression. These findings suggest that PPARγ-associated pathways may represent an important regulatory interface linking metabolic and inflammatory processes, while emphasizing the complexity of their temporal and cell-specific regulation. This review synthesizes current evidence from experimental studies, human multi-omics investigations, and clinical research to provide an updated perspective on the role of PPARγ in coordinating lipid metabolism and neuroinflammation in AD. In addition, we discuss the major translational challenges and emerging therapeutic strategies, including selective PPARγ modulation, improved central nervous system delivery, and precision treatment approaches tailored to disease stage.

items.title: Enhancer-targeted CRISPR-A rescues haploinsufficiency and mutant phenotypes in organoid models of autism.
items.authors: George T Chen; Gayatri Nair; Aubrey J Osorio; Sandra M Holley; Kimiya Ghassemzadeh; Yixuan Zhou; Jose Gonzalez; Jacqueline M Martin
items.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable condition with diverse clinical presentations. Approximately 15% of the genetic susceptibility of ASD is imparted by de novo haploinsufficient mutations of major effect. We mapped enhancers of two high-confidence autism genes, CHD8 and SCN2A, and used CRISPR-based gene activation targeting enhancers (eCRISPR-A) in human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids to correct the effects of haploinsufficiency, taking advantage of the presence of a wild-type allele of each gene and endogenous gene regulation. Here we show that eCRISPR-A induced a sustained increase in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and cortical organoids, with rescue of gene expression levels and mutation-associated phenotypes, including gene expression and physiology. These data support gene activation via targeting enhancers of haploinsufficient genes as a therapeutic intervention in ASD and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

items.title: CD14 in glioblastoma and temozolomide resistance: what the evidence does and does not support.
items.authors: Ayesha Bibi; Beomwoo Lee; Jaeseok Choi; Changgyu Son; Kyunghee Ha; Sumaiya Othuman Ibrahim; Sunho Eom; Yuwen Li
items.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM), designated as central nervous system World Health Organization grade 4, is the most lethal adult brain tumor, with a median overall survival (OS) of 14.6 months despite resection, radiotherapy, and temozolomide (TMZ). The benefit of TMZ is largely confined to the 45 % of GBMs carrying a methylated O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) promoter, where, in 206 assessable patients from the pivotal Phase III trial (reported in 2005), adding TMZ to radiotherapy extended median OS from 15.3 to 21.7 months, whereas MGMT-unmethylated tumors derived no significant benefit; these are historical estimates from a single trial subset. Resistance arises through MGMT-mediated repair of O6-methylguanine, MSH6 loss or mutation affecting mismatch repair, glioma stem cell repopulation, and an immunosuppressive microenvironment enriched with CD14+ myeloid cells, including tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), monocytes, and monocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells. CD14 is a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored co-receptor for Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), expressed constitutively on monocytes, macrophages, and microglia and also by a subset of glioma cells. Because CD14 has no intracellular domain, it cannot signal independently of a partner receptor; CD14-dependent signaling through TLR4/MD-2 has been proposed to contribute to nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation, pro-survival transcription, MGMT-related resistance pathways, and immunosuppressive myeloid polarization, although no study has shown this in glioma cells, the link to TMZ resistance remains hypothetical, and CD14 alone does not define an M2-like TAM phenotype. This review synthesizes over 50 publications across CD14 biology in the brain, CD14 expression across the immune and tumor-cell landscape of GBM, CD14-associated inflammatory signaling, TMZ resistance mechanisms, CD14-related influences on TMZ sensitivity, and candidate therapeutic strategies. Of those strategies, only IC14 (atibuclimab) targets CD14 directly; TLR4, NF-κB, signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 and colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor inhibition, TAM repolarization, poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibition, and checkpoint blockade act on the partner receptor, on shared downstream nodes or on the CD14-enriched myeloid compartment, and are therefore described as CD14-associated rather than CD14-targeted. CD14+ myeloid populations are associated with aggressive GBM biology, whereas the proposed glioma-cell-intrinsic CD14 → TLR4/MD-2 → NF-κB → MGMT cascade rests on a single 2003 expression dataset and has never been tested by CD14 loss-of-function, gain-of-function, rescue or lineage-specific in vivo experiments. The purpose of this review is to document that gap and to specify the experiments that would close it, not to advocate CD14 as a therapeutic target.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Hypersensitivity to adrenomedullin in post-traumatic headache: a randomized crossover study.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Haidar M Al-Khazali; Zahra Hakimzadeh; Anna G Melchior; Berkay Alpay; Ksenija Cucanić; Annette M Fuchs; Messoud Ashina; Håkan Ashina
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Adrenomedullin (ADM), a vasoactive member of the calcitonin peptide family with receptor-signalling overlap with calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), has emerged as a candidate therapeutic target in migraine. Given the striking clinical parallels between migraine and persistent post-traumatic headache (PTH), we investigated whether ADM-responsive signalling contributes to migraine-like headache in adults with persistent PTH attributed to mild traumatic brain injury. We conducted a single-centre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-way crossover study in adults with persistent PTH and no pre-trauma history of migraine. On two experimental days separated by at least 7 days, participants received 20-minute intravenous infusions of ADM (19.9 pmol kg⁻¹ min⁻¹) and isotonic saline as the matched inactive comparator (placebo) in randomised sequence. Headache outcomes were recorded for 12 hours. The primary outcome was the within-participant incidence of experimentally induced migraine-like headache. The secondary outcome was the within-participant difference in baseline-corrected area under the curve (AUC) for headache intensity from 0 to 12 hours. Of 158 individuals assessed for eligibility, 21 were randomised, completed both periods and were analysed. Participants had a mean age of 34.3 years, 19 (90%) were female, and 18 (86%) reported a migraine-like phenotype. Migraine-like headache occurred in 17 of 21 participants (81%) after ADM and four of 21 (19%) following placebo. Fourteen participants developed migraine-like only after ADM and one only following placebo, yielding a paired absolute risk difference of 61.9 percentage points (95% CI 29.7-80.6; one-sided P < 0.001; two-sided P = 0.001). Baseline-corrected headache-intensity AUC was higher after ADM than placebo (median 1,110 [IQR 315-2205] versus 420 [-160 to 565]; P = 0.006). Median time to onset of migraine-like headache was 30 minutes after ADM and 390 minutes following placebo. Fifteen participants reported that the ADM-induced headache resembled their usual migraine-like headache episodes, and rescue medication was used by 10 participants after ADM and two after placebo. These findings identify pronounced responsiveness to ADM-linked signalling in persistent PTH and support the ADM pathway as a candidate target for mechanism-based therapeutic development, pending confirmation in independent cohorts and complementary preclinical studies.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Glial progenitor-like state is preferentially co-opted in glioblastoma and sustained by POU3F3.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Susana I Ramos; Mohammad Imran K Khan; Wan Sze Cheng; Balagopal Pai; Thenzing J Silva-Hurtado; Jorge Samanamud; Xi Chen; Kristin G Beaumont
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Oncofetal reprogramming in glioblastoma (GBM) relies on the co-option of still poorly defined pathways that are transiently active during brain development, thereby exposing therapeutically actionable vulnerabilities. To better characterize GBM biology in the context of neurodevelopment, we create an expanded human spatiotemporal multi-omic dataset that resolves both gliogenic and neurogenic lineage fate and assess oncofetal reprogramming at the tumor core and infiltrative margin in both primary and recurrent disease. Analyses reveal the preferential enrichment of a glial intermediate progenitor cell (gIPC)-like state, which is most reminiscent of third-trimester germinal matrix gIPCs, across tumor regions and in recurrence. We uncover EGFR and the long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) NRXN1-DT as co-opted gIPC-specific markers, demonstrate NRXN1-DT's clinical utility in GBM diagnostics, and prioritize POU3F3 as a gIPC-like oncofetal driver, confirming its regulatory role in NRXN1-DT enhancer activity, EGFR expression, and maintenance of GBM stem/progenitor-like properties. This study lays the groundwork for future investigations into targeting POU3F3 and other co-opted gliogenic drivers as GBM therapeutics.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: The blood-brain barrier imports diverse neuroprotective proteins through pathways impaired early in Alzheimer's disease models.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Haoyue Zhou; Jason C Maynard; Alexander J Pennacchio; Amanda Apolonio; Xi Liu; Lei Yao; Mina Negahban; Zimo Zhang
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) has been defined primarily by what it excludes, yet the scale and function of physiological blood-to-brain protein transport remain largely unknown. Using bioorthogonal proteomics, we find that the healthy BBB samples 191 plasma proteins and permits 92 into the brain parenchyma. Enriched for carrier and metabolic functions, these proteins home to distinct brain cell types, such as apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1) to astrocytes and alpha-1 antitrypsin (SERPINA1) to microglia. This cell-type tropism relies on a BBB-parenchyma receptor hand-off: APOA1 crosses the BBB via SR-B1 and engages astrocytic ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), a key Alzheimer's risk gene, driving cholesterol efflux that supports synapse integrity. Unlike LPS-induced nonspecific leakage, early-stage 5xFAD mice show selective BBB transport remodeling, with reduced APOA1 and increased SERPINA1 uptake. Hepatic APOA1 overexpression restores APOA1 in the 5xFAD brain, rescuing astrocytic, synaptic, and behavioral deficits. These findings recast the BBB as a selective interface that recruits neuroprotective circulatory proteins for brain health.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Measles-like hypermutation of a Newcastle disease virus drives fatal encephalitis during BCMA × CD3 T-cell-redirecting immunotherapy.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Christina Krueger; Christoph Schaefers; Thomas Guenther; Lisa Leypoldt; Ricardo Ahrens; Winfried Alsdorf; Maximilian Al-Bazaz; Katja Weisel
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Newcastle disease virus (NDV or AOaV-1) is an avian paramyxovirus that typically causes only mild, self-limiting disease in humans. Here, we report fatal neuroinvasive AOaV-1 infection in a patient with multiple myeloma receiving maintenance therapy with teclistamab, daratumumab, and lenalidomide following frontline teclistamab-based treatment and autologous stem cell transplantation. Following rapidly progressive brainstem-cerebellar encephalitis and negative conventional microbiological testing, unbiased metagenomic RNA sequencing of a cerebellar biopsy identified AOaV-1 at high intraparenchymal abundance. Viral genome analysis revealed striking A-to-G and U-to-C substitutions selectively concentrated in the matrix gene, consistent with ADAR-mediated RNA editing. Long-read sequencing resolved two genetically distinct, independently hypermutated CNS haplotypes. Post-mortem analysis demonstrated widespread dissemination and continued viral diversification in multiple brain regions, whereas a peripheral urine sample contained a minimally mutated putative ancestral lineage. These findings support peripheral infection followed by CNS seeding and compartmentalized within-host evolution. The selective matrix-gene hypermutation closely parallels persistent measles virus infection in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, revealing a shared mechanism of paramyxovirus adaptation to the CNS. Profound immunotherapy-associated immune dysfunction may thus create niches enabling normally low-pathogenic zoonotic viruses to persist, evolve, and acquire severe neurovirulence.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Mesoscale molecular architecture of the striatum across cell types and adult aging.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Andrew W Kraft; Matthew Lee; Haoyuan Gao; Abir Mohsin; Nirmala A Rayan; Alyssa J Lawler; Garam Kim; Julianna Milidantri
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: The human striatum governs diverse motor, cognitive, and affective behaviors yet lacks the obvious cytoarchitectural boundaries defining functional territories elsewhere in the brain. Using Slide-tags single-nucleus spatial transcriptomics, we profiled 1.1 million cells across 19 postmortem donors to uncover the striatum's spatial organization. These data revealed a consistent subdivision of the striatum into six zones, each defined by molecularly distinct populations of spiny projection neurons (SPNs) and featuring spatially coordinated neuron-astrocyte interaction networks. To determine their structural relevance, we generated a companion mouse spatial atlas that identified four homologous zones that aligned with territories defined by brain-wide afferent projections. Finally, imputing zonal identities onto a 131-donor single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) cohort revealed that dorsal zones exhibit the greatest age-related transcriptional change and that the expression differences defining zonation attenuate with age. This resource establishes a conserved mesoscale spatial framework for the mammalian striatum, linking single-cell molecular identity to structural connectomics and aging.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: The genetic landscape of canine tumors: Insights from the Canine Cancer Genome Atlas (CCGA).
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Eugenio Mazzone; Laura Marconato; Antonella Fanelli; Luciano Cascione; Francesco Bertoni; Caterina Marchiò; Anna Sapino; Luca Aresu
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: The Canine Cancer Genome Atlas (CCGA, https://caninecancergenomeatlas.org/) is an open, accessible comparative oncology resource that harmonizes whole-exome data across 10 canine tumor histotypes. It aggregates 667 tumor-normal pairs with curated single-nucleotide variants, insertions and deletions, structural variants, and copy number aberrations. Cohort-depth stratification distinguished primary, exploratory, and descriptive analyses. Selection analyses identified 39 cancer drivers, including recurrent TP53, PIK3CA, PTEN, SETD2, MAP3K14, and FAT4 alterations; copy number events included MYC amplifications and PTEN deletions. Direct comparison with matched human cancers revealed conserved and species-enriched oncogenic mechanisms, pathways, and therapeutic contexts. The CCGA standardizes alignment, variant calling, and annotation through consensus pipelines and provides downloadable data and interactive analyses. This reusable framework advances precision veterinary oncology and strengthens translational bridges to human cancer, supporting comparative and translational research.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Neuronal cell-cycle re-entry stratifies clinical trajectories in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: The clinical heterogeneity of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) remains a fundamental barrier to effective therapy. While cell cycle re-entry in post-mitotic neurons is a known precursor to neurodegeneration, its role in defining patient-specific outcomes has never been established. Here, we integrate large-scale transcriptomic profiling from the AnswerALS cohort with mechanistic studies in human iPSC-derived spinal motor neurons to define how cell-cycle re-entry shapes disease heterogeneity in ALS. We identify a transcriptionally distinct patient subgroup with the highest expression of G1 or G2-phase cyclins that exhibit significantly slower functional decline (ALSFRS-R), whereas the engagement of S-phase markers correlates with accelerated disease progression. Nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction, a hallmark of ALS and related disorders, disrupts the spatial distribution of key regulatory proteins and may contribute to maladaptive cell-cycle activation. Our recent evidence suggests that impaired nuclear import may initiate, rather than merely accompany, neuronal cell-cycle re-entry. Using iPSC-derived motor neurons, we show that impaired nuclear import initiates TDP-43 pathology and global nuclear/cytoplasmic mis-localization of key ALS-related proteins. This nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction triggers a transient wave of cell-cycle activity immediately preceding neuronal cell death. Crucially, we show that DNA-replication initiation is a pathological inflection point of no return, as neurons entering S-phase accumulate replication-associated DNA damage and undergo cell death. Selective inhibition of CDK4/6 prevents S-phase entry and confers potent neuroprotection. Our findings demonstrate that impaired nuclear import drives maladaptive cell-cycle reactivation in ALS and that the depth of cell-cycle engagement stratifies neuronal fate and patient trajectories.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Expanding the genetic landscape of moyamoya angiopathy: insights from 74 trios.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Chaker Aloui; Manoelle Kossorotoff; Dominique Hervé; Markus Kraemer; Florence Riant; Stéphanie Guey; Juyeon Ko; Jinsung Kim
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Moyamoya angiopathy (MMA) is a rare cerebrovascular disorder characterized by progressive stenosis of intracranial arteries and the development of abnormal collateral vessels. While RNF213 is a major susceptibility gene in East Asian populations, the genetic architecture of MMA beyond RNF213, particularly in Europeans, remains largely undefined beyond a few known syndromic causes. We performed whole-exome sequencing on 74 sporadic MMA trios (proband and unaffected parents) of predominantly European ancestry. An additional cohort of 200 probands was screened for gene recurrence. We applied a stringent filtering strategy to identify de novo and rare inherited variants, followed by gene prioritization based on structural modeling, expression data, and biological plausibility. Gene-based burden tests were conducted against large control databases (gnomAD). We identified causative variants in 20 of the 74 probands (27%). Six probands with severe syndromic infant-onset phenotypes harbored de novo variants in the E3 ligase domain of RNF213. Fourteen probands carried a causative copy number variant (n = 3) or a short variant (n = 11) in a known MMA-associated gene (CBL, NF1, PTPN11, DIAPH1, ANO1, JAG1, NOS3, HBB). Beyond these established genes, we identified strong candidate variants in 11 probands from the discovery cohort, involving 11 novel candidate genes. Screening the additional cohort of 200 unrelated MMA probands identified recurrence of the gain-of-function SMAD4 p.Arg496Cys variant, which was de novo in the discovery-cohort proband, linking MMA to dysregulated TGF-β signaling. Other candidate findings included de novo loss-of-function variants in genes regulating epigenetic modulation and RNA splicing (SETD2, HNRNPL, UBAP2L, TOP2B, PRPF40A) and variants affecting vascular stress response (EPAS1, SVEP1, PDCD4). RNF213 was the only gene reaching exome-wide significance in burden testing (P = 2.11 × 10⁻11). This study establishes that MMA in non-East Asian populations is characterized by a strong genetic heterogeneity. These findings expand the molecular landscape of MMA and highlight the utility of trio-based sequencing for uncovering very rare molecular players in this disease. Additional analyses will now be needed to investigate the convergence of MMA pathways.

global_hot_topics.title: Mitochondrial protein import stress augments α-synuclein aggregation and neural damage.
global_hot_topics.authors: Liam P Coyne; Arnav Rana; Xiaowen Wang; Joseph Mauro; Sanaea Bhagwagar; Yumiko Umino; Eduardo C Solessio; Frank Middleton
global_hot_topics.abstract: Genetic and environmental factors are known to converge on mitochondria to cause Parkinson's disease. The underlying mechanism is incompletely understood. In addition to bioenergetic defects, nonbioenergetic pathways have been largely unexplored. Validating the nonbioenergetic mitochondrial stressors as independent pathogenic factors is challenging because most mouse models of mitochondrial stress are confounded by bioenergetic defects. Here, we show that expression of Ant1P.A114P,A123D, previously shown to cause mitochondrial protein import clogging in cultured human cells, does not affect the overall bioenergetic capacity, yet it induces proteostatic stress responses in the cytosol that suggests accumulation of unimported precursor proteins. In a Parkinson's disease model expressing α-synuclein (A53T), Ant1P.A114P,A123D increased the size of α-synuclein aggregates, increased aggregation of mitochondrial preproteins, heightened neuroinflammation, and worsened motor coordination defects. Importantly, we found no evidence of bioenergetic defects in either α-synuclein (A53T) or α-synuclein (A53T) + Ant1P.A114P,A123D mice. These data suggest that Ant1P.A114P,A123D likely induces mitochondrial protein import stress, and contributes to neural damage through cytosolic proteostatic stress and altered aggregation dynamics of neuropathogenic proteins independent of bioenergetics.

global_hot_topics.authors: Ting Li; Shun Han; Rui Chen; Lujin Li; Bin Wu
global_hot_topics.abstract: AIMS: To characterize the time course and influencing factors of placebo response in randomized trials of biologic and targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (tsDMARDs) for ankylosing spondylitis (AS). PATIENTS AND METHODS: We systematically searched major electronic databases (up to June 14, 2024) for randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trials of biologics or Janus kinase inhibitors in AS. Model-based meta-analysis with nonlinear mixed-effects modeling was conducted to pool placebo-arm ASAS20 (≥20% improvement by Assessment of SpondyloArthritis International Society criteria) and ASAS40 (≥40% improvement) response trajectories, using an exponential rise-to-maximum model with covariate screening and model validation. RESULTS: Thirty-eight trial arms from 36 trials (3046 placebo-treated participants) were included. The estimated maximum response (Pmax) was 31.1% for ASAS20 (90% of Pmax reached at 6.5 weeks) and 18.6% for ASAS40 (90% of Pmax reached at 17.0 weeks). ASAS20 Pmax increased by 2.7% per publication year. Smaller trials, no background therapy, lower male proportion, and lower baseline HLA-B27 positivity were associated with higher placebo response. CONCLUSIONS: The AS placebo response, particularly for ASAS20, shows a significant upward secular trend. This model provides a quantitative benchmark for trial design, anomalous placebo responses identification, and interpreting efficacy in trials lacking a concurrent placebo arm. Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a long-term inflammatory disease that mainly affects the joints of the spine. To find out whether a new medicine works, researchers compare it with a placebo, a dummy treatment with no active drug. The difficulty is that people given a placebo often improve anyway, and by very different amounts from trial to trial. When the placebo response is unusually large, an effective medicine can look as though it does not work. We collected data from 38 published AS trials of biologic medicines or Janus kinase inhibitors, covering 3046 people who received a placebo. Using a mathematical model, we described how the placebo response changes with time and what makes it larger or smaller. Two findings stood out. First, the placebo response grows slowly and then levels off: it takes about 6.5 weeks to reach its maximum when improvement reaches 20% and about 17 weeks when it reaches a stricter 40%, so a trial that stops early may underestimate the placebo group’s improvement. Second, the placebo response has grown by about 2.7% a year since 2002. It also tends to be larger in smaller trials, in trials where background painkillers were not allowed, in trials with fewer men and in trials where fewer patients carried the human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27) gene. Our model is a reference point: it helps researchers judge whether a new trial’s placebo response is unusually large or small, and interpret trials that had no placebo group. It may help design smaller, faster trials.

global_hot_topics.title: PIKfyve inhibition induces LRRK2 activation through phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate and CASM.
global_hot_topics.authors: Tomoki Kuwahara; Gen Yoshii; Maria Sakurai; Shoichi Suenaga; Hiroki Nakanishi; Matthew Jefferson; Thomas Wileman; Kentaro Tomii
global_hot_topics.abstract: LRRK2 is a Parkinson's disease-associated kinase that phosphorylates Rab GTPases. Hyperactivation of LRRK2, which is thought to cause Parkinson's disease, occurs on stressed endolysosomal membranes via conjugation of ATG8 to single membranes (CASM) and Rab, whereas the involvement of specific membrane lipids remained unclear. Here, we found that the inhibition of PIKfyve that metabolizes phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) induces hyperactivation of LRRK2 and that additional inhibition of the class III phosphoinositide 3-kinase that generates PI3P suppressed LRRK2 hyperactivation. Cellular PI3P levels were indeed elevated when LRRK2 was activated. CASM-induced activation of LRRK2, but not CASM itself, was suppressed by phosphoinositide 3-kinase inhibitors, whereas inhibition of CASM or Rab12/Rab29 suppressed LRRK2 activation induced by PIKfyve inhibitors. LRRK2 and phospho-Rab10 were colocalized with PI3P on LAMP1-positive enlarged vacuoles, and LRRK2 directly bound PI3P in vitro via its N-terminal positively charged amino acids. Together, we propose an updated mechanism of LRRK2 hyperactivation that simultaneously requires CASM, Rab, and PI3P-rich membranes.

global_hot_topics.title: Gene therapy for epilepsy: From
global_hot_topics.authors: Ruotong Qin; Xiaoge Hu; Wei Jiang; Jing Wang; Mei Zheng; Zhenqiang Zhang; Dongrui Ma
global_hot_topics.abstract: Genetic epilepsy, for which the molecular mechanisms are relatively well defined in numerous monogenic forms, represents an attractive model for the transition from symptomatic seizure control to mechanism‑driven correction. However, gene therapy strategies differ in their mechanisms of action, adaptability to specific mutations and translational maturity, making rational selection of interventions based on variant‑specific functional consequences an important clinical challenge. The present review examined five nucleic acid‑based therapeutic strategies, namely gene supplementation, enhancement of endogenous gene expression, gene silencing, DNA editing and RNA editing, for major causative genes, using mutation‑specific functional consequences [loss‑of‑function (LOF) vs. gain‑of‑function] as the primary framework for therapeutic decision‑making. The mechanisms and suitability of each approach are analysed, and their performance in terms of cell‑type specificity, delivery vectors and safety is evaluated by integrating evidence from animal models, induced pluripotent stem cell‑derived neurons and organoids and clinical trials. The present review also summarised key translational barriers, including vector cargo constraints, blood‑brain barrier penetration, off‑target and immune‑associated risks, therapeutic dosing windows and the timing of developmental intervention. Antisense oligonucleotides and regulatory adeno‑associated viral approaches, supported by mature delivery platforms and manageable safety profiles, have progressed furthest towards clinical validation. Endogenous gene activation strategies, such as CRISPR activation, offer a gene replacement‑free approach for LOF disorders but remain preclinical. DNA and RNA editing, while potentially capable of durable disease modification, require further evidence on delivery efficiency and long‑term homeostatic safety. Gene therapy for genetic epilepsy is undergoing a key transition from proof‑of‑concept studies to individualised clinical application. Future progress will depend on integrating personalised intervention design, multi‑target therapeutic combinations, artificial intelligence‑assisted sequence optimisation and standardised translational models, with the potential to drive a paradigm shift from seizure suppression to mechanistic correction.

global_hot_topics.title: Semantic Processing in Unresponsive Patients With Acute Brain Injury.
global_hot_topics.authors: Ayham Alkhachroum; Brian Manolovitz; John McKeown; Ana Bolanos; Elena Mishkovsky; Julia Houshmand; Gabriela Aklepi; Mariana Barrios
global_hot_topics.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Early prognostication after acute brain injury (ABI) is challenging because behavioral responsiveness may not accurately reflect preserved cognitive function. Neural responses to semantic incongruity can identify language processing despite the absence of overt behavior. We investigated whether bedside EEG could detect semantic processing in unresponsive patients with ABI and whether its presence was associated with long-term outcomes. METHODS: In this prospective 2-center cohort study, unresponsive adults with ABI admitted to neurologic intensive care units between 2022 and 2025 underwent bedside EEG during a language paradigm comparing congruent and incongruent sentence endings (e.g., "my favorite color is green/soon"). Semantic processing was defined by differential event-related responses within centroparietal channels (300-500 milliseconds) using cluster-based permutation testing with false discovery rate correction. Outcomes were assessed for recovery of consciousness and functional recovery (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended score ≥4) at 12 months by blinded interviewers. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, accuracy, and likelihood ratios. RESULTS: Among 105 patients (mean age 58 ± 19 years; 21% women; 53% Hispanic/Latino), the most common etiologies were intracerebral hemorrhage (45%), traumatic brain injury (43%), and subarachnoid hemorrhage (10%). Withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy occurred in 31%. Semantic processing was detected in 13 patients (12%). Recovery of consciousness occurred in 77% of patients with semantic processing compared with 49% without semantic processing (odds ratio [OR] 3.5; 95% CI 0.9-13.5, p = 0.08). Functional recovery occurred in 42% with semantic processing compared with 14% without semantic processing (OR 4.5; 95% CI 1.2-16.6, p = 0.03). Semantic processing was highly specific but insensitive for predicting both recovery of consciousness (specificity 94%, sensitivity 18%) and functional recovery (specificity 92%, sensitivity 29%). After excluding patients who underwent withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy or died of non-neurologic medical complications, specificity increased to 100% for recovery of consciousness and 95% for functional recovery. DISCUSSION: EEG evidence of semantic processing can be detected in a subset of unresponsive patients with ABI during the acute phase of injury and is associated with favorable long-term outcomes. Semantic processing was a specific but insensitive biomarker of recovery, suggesting potential utility as a rule-in marker of preserved cognitive function. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multicenter cohorts before clinical implementation.

global_hot_topics.title: Perioperative dynamics of selenoproteins and risk of cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury.
global_hot_topics.authors: Xian Xie; Wenbo Xue; Zeyang Wang; Zhi Li; Wei Feng; Hao Zhang; Wei Zhang
global_hot_topics.abstract: Cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury (CSA-AKI) affects over 20% of patients and is associated with perioperative mortality and long-term renal impairment. Reliable early biomarkers remain limited. Selenoproteins, including glutathione peroxidases (GPX1, GPX3) and selenoprotein P (SEPP1), are critical for redox homeostasis, but their perioperative changes in CSA-AKI remain unclear. This study aimed to characterize selenoprotein dynamics and explore their association with renal function and CSA-AKI. In this prospective observational cohort study, 99 adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery were enrolled, serum and urine samples were collected preoperatively and at 24/48 h postoperatively. SEPP1, GPX1, GPX3, and KIM-1 were measured. Mixed-effects, correlation, and logistic regression assessed selenoprotein dynamics and associations with CSA-AKI, with an exploratory model including age and preoperative SEPP1. Among 89 analyzed patients, 22 (24.7%) developed AKI. Univariable analyses showed that lower perioperative SEPP1 levels, attenuated urinary SEPP1 increases, and greater serum GPX1 decreases were associated with higher odds of CSA-AKI; older age, hypertension, and longer operation time were also associated with CSA-AKI. Postoperatively, serum SEPP1 declined markedly, remaining lower in AKI patients. Urinary SEPP1 increased significantly in non-AKI patients. Changes in GPX1 and GPX3 differed between AKI and non-AKI groups. Serum SEPP1 correlated positively with eGFR and inversely with creatinine and cystatin C. An exploratory model incorporating age and preoperative serum SEPP1 yielded an apparent AUC of 0.818. In summary, perioperative alterations in selenoproteins (GPX1, GPX3, SEPP1) are closely linked to CSA-AKI. Preoperative SEPP1 combined with clinical variables may enable early risk prediction and support timely intervention. Acute kidney injury is a common complication after cardiac surgery. Selenoproteins help regulate antioxidant defense and responses to physiological stress, but their changes around cardiac surgery are not well understood.In this prospective study of 89 adults undergoing cardiac surgery, 22 developed acute kidney injury. In 54 patients with biomarker measurements, we assessed three selenoproteins—SEPP1, GPX1, and GPX3—in blood and urine before and after surgery.Patients who developed acute kidney injury showed different perioperative selenoprotein patterns, including lower serum SEPP1 levels and altered GPX1 and GPX3 responses. Higher serum SEPP1 was generally associated with better kidney function, and preoperative serum SEPP1 showed potential value for risk assessment when combined with age.These findings suggest that selenoproteins may provide additional information about kidney vulnerability after cardiac surgery. medical_news.abstract: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.

medical_news.title: Scientists wipe out deadly brain tumors in every mouse tested with new cancer therapy
medical_news.abstract: Scientists at UC San Francisco have developed a powerful new cancer therapy that remains inactive until it reaches the brain, where it switches on to attack deadly tumors. The engineered immune cells, called B-SYNC CAR-T cells, completely eliminated diffuse midline glioma (DMG), an aggressive childhood brain cancer that is almost always fatal within a year, in two mouse models.

medical_news.title: Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders
medical_news.abstract: Scientists have discovered that sleep disorders are associated with structural changes in brain regions that control attention, decision-making, and emotions, potentially explaining why disrupted sleep can affect everyday thinking and behavior. The findings, drawn from 57 brain imaging studies, reveal both shared and disorder-specific patterns that could lead to more targeted treatments.

medical_news.title: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
medical_news.abstract: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop.

Researchers found that women taking an oxaloacetate supplement for eight weeks experienced substantial improvements in memory, concentration, mental clarity, and fatigue.

medical_news.title: Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't
medical_news.abstract: Yale researchers have discovered that certain prescription drugs, healthy diets, and exercise can measurably slow biological aging, while popular anti-aging supplements appear largely ineffective.
